description: We're third-year Software Engineering student at Concordia with experience building full-stack applications, AI-powered tools, and interactive dashboards. We are interested in tackling Flame in Freefall and building something practical, polished, and technically sound.
summary: NASA’s Moon Base will likely run at 30% oxygen or more. Firebreak shows how much flight evidence exists for that. It’s a web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets the 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system. Pick a habitat scenario (ISS cabin air, Moon Base, pressurized rover, Exploration Atmosphere or spacesuit) and Firebreak ranks the investigations and matching flight runs with deterministic code, then shows exactly where the evidence runs out. Of the 263 flight runs we imported from PSI, the 140 solid-material runs with a recorded starting oxygen top out at 22.2%, and none were in lunar or Martian gravity. We imported the data without correcting it: values the source can’t support are flagged, and 6 disagreements between PSI tables and NASA’s own papers are shown side by side. An AI assistant answers questions only with quotes verified word for word against NASA sources (90 of 90 in our evaluation), and declines when the sources don’t cover the question. Firebreak gives no risk scores; it shows planners which questions NASA’s data can answer, and which it can’t yet.
details:
What it does
Firebreak shows what NASA has burned in space, and what it hasn’t. NASA’s Moon Base will likely run at 30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi. Firebreak lets a mission planner pick a habitat scenario (ISS cabin air, Moon Base, pressurized rover, NASA’s Exploration Atmosphere, or a spacesuit) and see which of the 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system have evidence close to it, which real flight runs match, and exactly where the evidence runs out.

The data, and how we treated it
We imported 263 flight runs from five PSI run tables (BASS-II, BASS, Saffire-I, Saffire-II and Saffire-III). The raw files are never edited. Where a value can’t be supported by its source, the run is flagged, never corrected: 216 of the 263 runs carry at least one visible data-quality flag. Reading the source columns carefully mattered. The BASS-II table has a fan-potentiometer column and an airflow column, and our importer reads airflow from the correct one, so every BASS-II airflow is a physical speed of 53 cm/s or less. Cross-checking the PSI tables against NASA’s own published papers, we found 6 discrepancies. We kept the PSI value and show the paper’s value beside it.

The result: of the imported solid-material runs, 140 record a starting oxygen, and the highest is 22.2%. None of the 263 runs were in lunar or Martian gravity. The Evidence Gap Atlas makes this visible: 6 of 35 atmosphere–material combinations have a matching flight run, and every match is in ISS cabin air.

How it works

  • Scenario Lab: deterministic code ranks investigations by closeness on material, oxygen, airflow and gravity, and shows the matching runs, a gap chart, recorded flammability limits (17 limit points, with 10 ambiguous ones excluded and the reasons published), and what varied or was held fixed within each investigation. When a scenario falls outside the tested conditions, Firebreak says so and why, and does not extrapolate.
  • Ask the evidence: questions are answered only from retrieved NASA text (PSI pages, NASA pages and published NASA papers). Server code checks every quote word for word against its source before the answer is shown. If nothing verifies, the answer says the sources don’t cover the question.
  • Measured, not assumed: a public scorecard on 28 fixed questions: 27 got the expected result, 90 of 90 citations were verified, and 6 of 7 unanswerable questions were declined. The one miss is shown, not tuned away. Claim checks re-verify every number we state against the data on each build.
  • Hardware watchlist: 15 ISS hardware items from NASA’s 2026 NESC assessment of Exploration atmospheres (NTRS 20260003925), each with NASA’s own sentence beside the PSI flight evidence for that material.
  • Earth applications: suppression, smoke detection and firefighter gear, linking PSI records and NASA Spinoffs.

Impact
Firebreak doesn’t produce risk scores or safety verdicts. It shows engineers and mission planners which questions NASA’s flight data can answer and which it can’t yet, so the next tests (such as the lunar experiments LUCI and FM2) can target the gaps.

What makes it different
Code ranks the evidence and the AI only explains retrieved text. Every number on the site is traceable to a source file, every quote is verified, and the app publishes its own error rate.

Tools
Next.js, TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, MiniSearch (retrieval), Zod, Vitest (393 tests), three.js and GSAP (intro animation), the Vercel AI SDK with OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini, deployed on Vercel.

Use of AI

  • In the product: the Ask page uses OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini to write answers from retrieved NASA text, and server code drops any quote that doesn’t match its source word for word. All ranking, matching, gap detection and numbers are computed by deterministic code from NASA data, not by AI.
  • In building it: Anthropic Claude (Claude Code and Claude chat) helped with planning, code, tests, data-pipeline checks and writing. We reviewed every change against acceptance checks.
  • In the video: the narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs), and this is noted on screen.
  • Data and images: no NASA data, values or quotes were generated by AI. The Earth image is NASA’s Blue Marble.
